label: Wasps, hornets and other stinging insects
summary: Yellowjackets, hornets and paper wasps defend their nests in numbers, and a wasp's stinger has no barbs, so each one can sting again and again. Nests hide in wall and ceiling voids, attics, eaves, trees, equipment left standing and old rodent burrows in the ground, so disturbing one can set off an attack. Most stings just hurt, but a sting can kill someone allergic, and many stings at once can make anyone ill.
signs: Wasps flying in and out of one spot, such as a hole in the ground or a gap in a building: that points to a nest
Grey paper nests under eaves, in attics, in trees and shrubs, or on equipment left standing, such as ladders
Yellowjackets mostly nest in holes in the ground, often old rodent burrows, and also in wall and ceiling voids
Late summer and fall: colonies are larger (1,500 to 15,000 wasps, depending on species), food is scarcer and wasps get more defensive
do: Before lifting, opening or dragging anything that has stood outside, such as a ladder, mower, appliance or tarp, look for wasps flying in and out of it: that points to a nest
Deal with nests, or move things near them, in the evening or at night, when wasps are in the nest and least active; they can still sting in the dark, so put a red filter over your torch
Cover up: light-coloured, smooth clothing over as much skin as possible, and a head net near a nest; skip scented soap and perfume
If one wasp is around you, stay calm and still
If they start stinging, run: get well away from the nest, indoors or into shade if you can
Anyone with a known sting allergy should carry their auto-injector and medical ID, and tell the group where it is
A nest that isn't in your way can wait: Health Canada says it's best left until November or December
dont: Don't swat: it can make them sting
Don't jump into water to escape: some stinging insects hover over the water
Don't squeeze a stinger or pull it out with tweezers
Don't let someone having a severe reaction stand up or walk, even if they feel better
Don't take antihistamine tablets instead of epinephrine: Canada's immunization guide says they shouldn't be used in the first treatment of anaphylaxis
ppe: Light-coloured, smooth-finished clothing covering as much skin as possible
A head net and protective clothing when you must go near a nest
firstAid: Get away from the nest first. Scrape any stinger out sideways with a fingernail or card edge, wash with soap and water, cool with a wrapped ice pack or cold wet cloth for up to 20 minutes, raise the limb, and don't scratch

Have someone stay with them and watch for anaphylaxis, which usually starts within minutes: trouble breathing or a swollen tongue or throat, or signs in two or more of skin (rash, swelling), breathing (high-pitched noises), alertness (dizziness, fainting) and stomach (vomiting)

If they have an auto-injector, use it first: push it firmly against the outer thigh until it clicks, hold it in place as directed (usually 5–10 seconds), rub the spot for 30 seconds; repeat the dose after 5 minutes if they are no better

With or without one: lie them down with legs raised, or sit them up slowly if breathing is hard; don't let them stand or walk. If they pass out but breathe normally, roll them onto their side; if they stop breathing normally, start CPR
Being stung more than once, or in the mouth, throat or near the eyes, needs medical help even without an allergy
